items.title: Statement From NVIDIA Board of Directors
items.raw_content: The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board said it has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, and that Jensen supports the review.
items.title_zh: 英伟达董事会就黄仁勋遭外国情报活动瞄准的报道启动独立调查
items.summary: NVIDIA's board said it is launching an independent investigation after reports that founder and CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, with a committee of independent directors and outside counsel overseeing it.

items.title: New ID. AURA is the mainstream EV VW needs – but its software is the real story
items.raw_content: Volkswagen built its global empire on the promise of affordable, accessible transportation, embodied by the iconic Type 1 Beetle. Now facing an existential crisis after a decades-long push upmarket , the automaker faces a reckoning – and a retreat back into affordable, mass-market electric sedans like the new FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 (and the software that powers it) might be exactly what VW needs to reach a new generation of buyers. more…
items.title_zh: 大众 ID. AURA 面向主流电动车市场，软件成为真正看点
items.summary: Volkswagen's FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 is a mass-market electric sedan aimed at reversing the automaker's push upmarket, and Electrek argues its software platform is the more important story for reaching new buyers.

items.title: French carmaker Renault wants to get into the military robot business
items.raw_content: Forget what your Fox News -addicted uncle told you about cheese-eating surrender monkeys. The French military has centuries of storied military victories and traditions behind it, and Renault wants in on that action with a new, autonomous electric vehicle platform designed to tackle the Armée de Terre’s most demanding missions. more…
items.title_zh: 雷诺进军军用机器人业务，推出自主电动平台
items.summary: Renault plans to enter the military robot business with a new autonomous electric vehicle platform designed for the French Army's demanding missions.

items.title: Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles
items.raw_content: If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove. Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here. more…
items.title_zh: 与其追逐电动皮卡，不如多造电动 125cc 摩托车
items.summary: An Electrek opinion piece argues that the EV industry's focus on electric SUVs and pickups overlooks the global need for affordable electric 125cc motorcycles, which are more relevant to how many people actually commute.

items.title: Android tablets are back, but are they for you?
items.raw_content: Android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling? 9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here . Sign up below to access the web version. more…
items.title_zh: 安卓平板回归：大屏产品是否适合你？
items.summary: 9to5Google's Weekender notes that Android tablets are making a comeback and asks readers whether the large-screen tablets brands are pushing actually fit their usage.

items.title: Here are the best electric bikes you can buy at every price level in November 2026
items.raw_content: I’ve spent countless hours here at Electrek doing detailed hands-on testing of hundreds of electric bikes. Through thousands of miles of riding, I’ve been fortunate to learn these e-bikes inside and out, top to bottom and front to back. That long-term experience with real-world e-bike testing has helped me find the best electric bicycles on the market for just about any budget. Below are some of the top e-bikes I’ve hand-tested for every price range, current as of November 2026. These are probably the best deals you’ll find all year on electric bikes, meaning this is the best time ever to get a new model! Check out the awesome e-bikes below, any one of which could become your next electric bike. more…

items.summary: Electrek published its November 2026 guide to the best electric bikes at every price level, based on hands-on testing across hundreds of models.

items.title: Apple aiming to make Siri ‘more like an agent’ as soon as next year: report
items.raw_content: Apple finally shipped its long awaited personalized Siri with iOS 27. The company lived up to its promises, and delivered on its hefty goals that it set out back in 2024. That said, Siri still lacks in terms of proactively taking actions for you, a feature that many AI companies are actively working towards. Apple might come around on that next year, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman . The company is also experimenting with a new engineering pipeline that might make faster development possible. more…
items.title_zh: 报道称苹果最早明年让 Siri 更像一个智能体
items.summary: According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple aims to make Siri more capable of taking actions on its own as soon as next year, and is experimenting with a new engineering pipeline that could speed development.

items.title: Report: John Ternus pushing Craig Federighi to speed up Apple software engineering

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , new Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly pushing on software chief Craig Federighi to ‘accelerate’ Apple’s roadmap for software. more…

items.title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
items.raw_content:
Authors: Zhiyu An, Yiping Li, Wan Du

Can high-bandwidth flash (HBF) make LLM inference cheaper than adding GPUs? By storing weights closer to the GPU than SSD, HBF may reduce the number of GPUs needed for model capacity. However, this integration is only justified if it meets service targets and its cost is recovered. We simulate this integration using public component data across nine dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, five workloads, two GPU platforms, and 1--100 GPUs. At fixed demand, HBF reduces the minimum GPU count to meet a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons; majority of them are paused and short sessions, 63 remain cost-effective at half a GPU price per HBF stack. For single short-chat users, HBF enables large MoEs, e.g. DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, to meet a relaxed service target on one RTX~4090 GPU, where conventional serving fails. At fixed GPU count, HBF improves throughput in 48\% of matched comparisons below 16 GPUs and 13\% at larger counts. Even at 100 RTX~4090-scale GPUs, cascaded HBF raises offline throughput by 16.4--26.5$\times$ for three large MoEs. We found savings and throughput gains arise in different scenarios.
items.title_zh: 高带宽闪存何时能让 LLM 推理比加 GPU 更便宜？
items.summary: A simulation study across nine dense and MoE models, five workloads and 1–100 GPUs finds that high-bandwidth flash reduces the minimum GPU count for meeting a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons, mostly for paused and short sessions, and can serve large MoEs on a single RTX 4090 for single short-chat users; at 100 GPUs, cascaded HBF raised offline throughput 16.4–26.5× for three large MoEs.

items.title: PRISM: Preference-based Reward and Uncertainty-Integrated Synthesis Minimization for RTL PPA Optimization
items.raw_content:
Authors: Armin Abdollahi, Negin Ashrafi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

This paper introduces a budget-aware, multi-objective framework (called PRISM) for RTL optimization that improves power, performance, and area (PPA) while sharply limiting expensive commercial synthesis tool calls. Starting from a synthesizable baseline and functional testbench, the method iterates through LLM-driven rewrite generation, fast compile/simulation equivalence filtering, low-cost proxy feature extraction, and selective commercial synthesis tool (Synopsys Design Compiler (DC)) evaluation. To prioritize which candidates deserve high-quality synthesis, we train a preference-based reward model using pairwise ranking supervision derived from commercial synthesis tool outcomes, and combine ensemble uncertainty with a diversity-aware acquisition rule to avoid early bias and redundant evaluations. A key advantage is that PRISM maintains a best-tradeoff set G of non-dominated designs throughout the run: G preserves the best solutions found so far, is fed back into generation and refinement, and enables consistent, cumulative improvements rather than repeatedly restarting from the baseline. Across RTLLM v2.0 modules, the approach consistently yields post-synthesis gains under fixed commercial synthesis tool call budgets, and ablations confirm that reward-guided selection and candidate dropping are central to sample-efficient progress. PRISM efficacy is evaluated across multiple technology nodes (7 nm, 15 nm, and 45 nm) using identical pipelines without retraining.
items.title_zh: PRISM：用偏好奖励模型减少 RTL 优化中的商用综合调用
items.summary: PRISM is a budget-aware multi-objective framework for RTL optimization that combines LLM-driven rewrites, fast equivalence filtering, proxy features and selective Synopsys Design Compiler runs, using a preference-based reward model and uncertainty-aware acquisition; it reports consistent post-synthesis PPA gains on RTLLM v2.0 across 7nm, 15nm and 45nm nodes without retraining.

items.title: ICLayout-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Custom Circuit Layout Design
items.raw_content:
Authors: Zhangmai Li, Tianrui Ma, Zheng Weng, Mo Zou, Zidong Du et al.

Large language model (LLM) agents are being explored for circuit design, but their ability to produce high-quality custom layouts has not been extensively evaluated. ICLayout-Bench is a benchmark in which agents use electronic design automation (EDA) tools to construct and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level circuit netlists. These layouts are evaluated using physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation. Layouts that pass the physical and functional checks are scored on electrical performance and area. The benchmark includes 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs), covering technology nodes from 3 nm to 180 nm. The tasks span analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits in open-source and commercial EDA flows. The experiments evaluate 22 configurations spanning seven models on 21 public and 19 private tasks. Mean layout scores range from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks, on a 100-point scale. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently improve mean scores, and configurations with comparable scores can incur substantially different model costs.
items.title_zh: ICLayout-Bench：评估 LLM 代理定制电路版图设计能力
items.summary: ICLayout-Bench evaluates LLM agents that use EDA tools to build and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level netlists, scoring physical verification, parasitic extraction, post-layout simulation, electrical performance and area across 165 tasks, 13 PDKs and 3nm–180nm nodes; across 22 configurations and seven models, mean scores ranged from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks.

items.title: Priority-Aware Deficit Round Robin for AXI4 Bandwidth Fairness in ASAP-7nm Process
items.raw_content:
Authors: Tasmin Khan, Tishna Sabrina, Ch. Md. Rakin Haider

Modern systems-on-chip place real-time clients, processor cores and bulk data engines on the same AXI4 interconnect, where they contend for shared slaves. AXI4 fixes the ordering rules and carries a 4-bit quality of service (QoS) field, but leaves the service policy to the implementer, and that policy determines how long each master waits and how much bandwidth it receives once a slave saturates. We propose a QoS-aware deficit round robin (DRR) architecture that charges each grant in beats, and benchmark it against two architectures built behind the same port list: round robin, and QoS priority with anti-starvation aging. Charging in beats recovers bandwidth fairness while leaving every burst whole, so the address phase is issued once and locality for memory access is preserved. All three are driven by the same deterministic traffic generator and taken from RTL to GDSII on the ASAP7 7-nm predictive PDK. Under a 1:16 burst-length mismatch, the round robin and QoS architectures both hold the beat ratio between the two competing masters at 1:16, while our design brings it to 1:1 at full load. Mean read latency for the priority master falls from 95 cycles under round robin to 67 with QoS and 37 with QoS-aware DRR. At 500 MHz this serves the priority master in 74 ns against 190 ns. The measurements give a per-policy price and a traffic-based guide for choosing among the three.
items.title_zh: 面向 AXI4 带宽公平性的优先级感知 DRR 架构
items.summary: A QoS-aware deficit round robin architecture for AXI4 interconnects charges each grant in beats to preserve bursts; on an ASAP7 7nm RTL-to-GDSII flow under a 1:16 burst-length mismatch, it brought the competing masters' beat ratio to 1:1 and cut the priority master's mean read latency from 95 cycles under round robin to 37 cycles.

items.title: CU-3D: A Scalable Legality-Aware RTL-to-GDS Flow for 3D-IC Physical Design
items.raw_content:
Authors: Mingjun Wang, Guanqi Li, Yihan Wen, Lancheng Zou, Mingjun Li et al.

Face-to-face (F2F) hybrid bonds shorten interdie connections, but data, clock, and power-grid (PG) connections must be realized together. CU-3D is a RTL-to-GDS physical design flow based on commercial EDA tools. It derives role-compatible hybrid-bond (HB) sites from a 17-metal ASAP7-based technology model, complete HB footprints, and constructed PG geometry. To coordinate partitioning with placement flexibility, Scaled refines an inherited 2D placement, whereas Fresh places the receiving die first and uses its pin locations and clock loads to guide placement of the other die. Data and clock HB assignments are jointly optimized while retaining alternative data sites and reserving capacity for subsequent PG assignment. The selected HB sites and stacks are preserved during 3D clock-tree synthesis, supply-aware cell insertion, and routing. Across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, the flow achieves zero backend DRC violations and passes signal-connectivity checks. Nine paired designs admit lower-footprint, lower-power implementations; four improve setup WNS. On JPEG, early joint planning gains 87 ps and mobility-aware partitioning gains 346 ps. Path analysis explains why cell-delay savings can outweigh net-delay increases.
items.title_zh: CU-3D：面向 3D-IC 物理设计的合法化 RTL-to-GDS 流程
items.summary: CU-3D is a commercial-EDA-based RTL-to-GDS flow for face-to-face hybrid-bond 3D-ICs that jointly plans data, clock and power-grid connections; across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, it reports zero backend DRC violations, passing connectivity checks, lower footprint and power on nine paired designs, and setup WNS improvements on four.

items.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
items.raw_content:
Authors: Zhengyang Cheng, He Zhu, Zeyu Guo, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu et al.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms.
  In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.
items.title_zh: Zora：用检索式推测与硬件加速提升 VLA 推理速度
items.summary: Zora is a hardware-software co-design framework that accelerates autoregressive vision-language-action inference using a lightweight RAG-based draft model, kinematics-guided action acceptance and KV-cache-sharing attention, plus dedicated hardware for irregular RAG memory access; on four VLA models and LIBERO it retained comparable accuracy with up to 3.4× software speedup and 7.6× with hardware support over GPUs.

items.title: Compute Regeneration through Re-Productization: Reorganizing Retired Edge AI Silicon into a Delivered Multilingual Service Robot
items.raw_content:
Authors: Hongyu Luo, Sun Tie, John Wang

Useful edge hardware can lose product support while retaining substantial computation. We treat this as systems design: compute regeneration here means re-productization, retaining the compute module while redesigning the surrounding product organization. Our case is GEdgeBot, a multilingual service robot built around a retired 32 GB Jetson AGX Xavier. A source-grounded inventory shows the box alone supplies inference, while the combined system exposes five on-device AI services, a seven-language speech chain, three sensing domains, and one deterministic seven-byte control boundary. AI and orchestration stay on the Xavier; finite motor-pulse generation on an STM32F407. Audits cover the six-mode control state machine, readiness barriers and sound orientation. Historical single-prototype measurements report 1,782 MB GPU memory with YOLO, Whisper-small, and NLLB-200 resident, a direct-control p99 deviation rising from 0.24 to 49.93 ms under concurrent AI load, and six of six trigger-to-follow demonstrations at 4.35 s mean latency, with conversational voice unavailable. A November campaign restores an isolated inference stack, re-measures AI workloads, and repeats control-frame runs. Driving two execution organisations with the same 6,000 measured 50 ms frame intervals shows the finite-pulse boundary removes host jitter from the pulse train but not the command start phase; its stopping bound is host-enforced, while the MCU 16-bit pulse field is unclamped. A six-check static audit exposes a host--MCU queue mismatch, and a 14-scenario replay executes the audited main() dispatcher across six modes with zero physical device opens and 54 contract-checked frames. Results support an existence claim and a reproducible architectural hypothesis, not fleet-level reliability. The 208 direct-control ratio remains unreplicated; MCU waveform capture and on-site fault injection remain open.
items.title_zh: GEdgeBot：把退役 Jetson 硬件重组为多语言服务机器人
items.summary: GEdgeBot is a multilingual service robot built around a retired 32GB Jetson AGX Xavier, combining five on-device AI services, a seven-language speech chain and three sensing domains while keeping motor-pulse generation on an STM32F407; the authors present it as a reproducible re-productization case, not a fleet-reliability claim.

items.title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
items.raw_content:
Authors: Sunghyeun Woo, Javier Conde, Pedro Reviriego

A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.
items.title_zh: 相同错误，不同恢复：错误呈现方式如何影响 LLM 代理行为
items.summary: A study across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters finds that the same tool error can lead to different retry, correction or stop behavior depending on how it is delivered; a new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoided severe stopping failures in Llama models and, as an opt-in recovery layer on ToolMaze, raised success on explicit errors by 14.2 points for 7–8B models and 10.5 points for 32–70B models.

items.title: Practical Deep Learning-Based Block Demapping for mmWave MIMO Systems
items.raw_content:
Authors: Syed Asrar ul haq, Jesus O. Lacruz, Joerg Widmer, Sumit J. Darak

Deep learning is expected to play a central role in 6G systems, by enabling data-driven physical layer designs that can adapt to practical wireless impairments. This is particularly important for millimetre-wave (mmWave) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which are strongly affected by residual channel distortions, interference, and hardware non-idealities that are difficult to capture with analytical models. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based soft demapper that performs block-wise processing of received symbols instead of conventional symbol-wise detection. The demapper employs a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to learn temporal structure induced by practical propagation and hardware effects, while producing soft bit outputs compatible with soft-decision decoding stages. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated for a 4$\times$4 wideband mmWave MIMO system at 60~GHz, using an over-the-air dataset collected across multiple days and settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over a conventional soft-decision demapper, including up to a 2.6$\times$ reduction in bit error rate for 16QAM and up to a 17.6$\times$ reduction for 64QAM under real over-the-air mmWave MIMO conditions. The proposed demapper is further implemented on a Zynq RFSoC platform using a reconfigurable convolution engine and fixed-point arithmetic, achieving an approximately 34.3$\times$ speedup compared to a processor-based implementation, and demonstrating that learning-based demapping can be deployed efficiently on resource-constrained edge hardware.
items.title_zh: 面向毫米波 MIMO 的深度学习块解映射器
items.summary: A deep-learning soft demapper for mmWave MIMO processes received symbols block-wise with a 1D CNN, producing soft bits for soft-decision decoding; on a 4×4 60GHz over-the-air dataset it reduced bit error rate by up to 2.6× for 16QAM and 17.6× for 64QAM versus a conventional demapper, and an FPGA implementation achieved about 34.3× speedup over a processor.

items.title: A Per-Step Load-Balancing Engine for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
items.raw_content:
Authors: Jingyuan Li, Maolin Wang, Hayden So

In expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, a layer finishes only when the most loaded GPU of its group does. Token routing shifts at every decode step and concentrates on a few experts, so most of the group's reserved GPU time waits on stragglers. Recovering that time means re-deciding, at every layer of every decode step, how each replicated expert's tokens divide between its copies. The exact linear-program solvers that make this decision optimally take longer than many of the layers they serve, and their working set outgrows GPU shared memory at deployment scale. We introduce Relief, a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that makes the linear program unnecessary, coming within a fraction of a point of the per-step optimum in a few passes of integer halving over the token counts. We build and measure three deployments, CUDA kernels on the serving GPU, the same verified engine on an FPGA over PCIe, and a fixed-function block beside the accelerator. On decode routing from three open MoE families, Relief holds the balance near the per-step optimum at every group size and layer time measured. Scored as effective utilization relative to that optimum, the kernel alone matches or exceeds every deployable scheme at every group size, from the hundred-microsecond layer on. The on-die engine widens that lead at every point, recovering up to 37.3 percentage points over the deployed static placement, while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.
items.title_zh: Relief：面向专家并行 MoE 服务的逐步负载均衡引擎
items.summary: Relief replaces exact linear-program solvers in expert-parallel MoE serving with a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that approaches the per-step optimum in a few integer-halving passes; across three open MoE families it matched or beat deployable schemes, and an on-die engine recovered up to 37.3 percentage points over static placement while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.

items.title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.raw_content:
Authors: Yunheng Wang, Jiaxi Zhang, Wei Lu, Yuetong Fang, Taowen Wang et al.

Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
items.title_zh: Kimodo-Policy：学习人形机器人移动操作的运动学动作模型
items.summary: Kimodo-Policy treats whole-body motion as a pretraining target, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with ControlNet visual conditioning and a root-body-hand hierarchy for humanoid loco-manipulation.

items.title: ForeAct: Geometry-Guided Action Learning from World Representations
items.raw_content:
Authors: Wei Lu, Jiaxi Zhang, Yunheng Wang, Taowen Wang, Yuetong Fang et al.

Robotic manipulation requires representations that capture both scene geometry and its evolution during interaction. Existing approaches have largely treated these two aspects separately. World action models capture such dynamics by coupling action prediction with future video generation, but their reliance on iterative diffusion or rectified-flow inference leads to high computational cost, while their representations lack explicit spatial structure. Explicitly modeling scene geometry typically requires auxiliary modules that increase both parameter count and computational cost. Conversely, geometry-centric policies primarily recover observed spatial structure and often lack explicit supervision for anticipating future geometric changes during interaction. To address these limitations, we introduce ForeAct, which repurposes a pretrained video world model as a single-pass representation backbone for low-latency control. ForeAct directly processes the clean latent of the current observation in one forward pass, eliminating future-frame synthesis and iterative denoising while retaining the backbone's pretrained spatiotemporal priors. Rather than introducing a separate geometry backbone, ForeAct uses learnable tokens supervised by next-frame relative depth to shape the shared video representation through bidirectional self-attention. This compact interface turns the spatial knowledge already encoded in the backbone into a future-aware representation for action generation, with little parameter overhead. The lightweight geometry readout is used only during training and removed at deployment, enabling low-latency, geometry-aware control without depth input or an external geometry backbone. Without additional large-scale pretraining, ForeAct achieves 96.6% average success on LIBERO, 63.5% on SimplerEnv-Bridge, and a 74.4% success rate across 90 real-world rollouts.
items.title_zh: ForeAct：从世界表示中学习几何引导的动作
items.summary: ForeAct repurposes a pretrained video world model as a single-pass representation backbone, avoiding future-frame synthesis and iterative denoising while retaining spatial structure for low-latency manipulation.

items.title: DriveFoundry: Co-Evolving Data and Model for Efficient Closed-Loop Iteration in Autonomous Driving
items.raw_content:
Authors: Ziyang Yao, Yuncheng Jiang, Fang Li, Haochen Liu, Shaoqing Xu et al.

A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
items.title_zh: DriveFoundry：面向自动驾驶的数据与模型闭环迭代
items.summary: DriveFoundry couples causal data refinement with adaptive inference; its Xiaomi-Drive-o1 model unifies perception, causation, action, world and value in a shared vision-language backbone for autonomous driving.

items.title: InfraRSI: Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure
items.raw_content:
Authors: InfraRSI Team, Yuchuan Tian, Haocheng Mei, Ye Yuan, Chao Xu et al.

While Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) accelerates isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, distributed LLM training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels, and communication schedules, where single edits often hit out-of-memory (OOM) boundaries, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter, or silent numerical drift. We present InfraRSI, the agentic harness that turns open-ended human commands into verified training optimizations via a five-stage workflow: init locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss, and timing invariants to prevent reward hacking, doctor profiles baseline phases and calibrates cluster noise, run co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches before re-verifying top candidates against the baseline and logging findings to a cross-hardware experience bank, and report and apply audit source paths, track failed-trial costs, and commit promoted changes. Rather than stepping greedily from a single incumbent, InfraRSI initializes from diverse experience-seeded configurations and fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials, including OOMs. Using these models, it prices per-setting memory costs, revises miscalibrated LLM priors from live runs, and pairs memory-hungry optimizations with memory savers and verified code patches. Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to $2.75\times$ and lifts mean Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from $17.4\%$ to $30.0\%$, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs. As it improves training infrastructure efficiency, InfraRSI forms a two-level Recursive Self-Improvement loop---revising priors online within runs and distilling experience across clusters---to push foundation model scaling.
items.title_zh: InfraRSI：用递归自我改进优化分布式训练基础设施
items.summary: InfraRSI is an agentic harness that turns human commands into verified training optimizations through a five-stage workflow covering scope locking, profiling, co-optimization, verification and audit.
